title: King and pawn against king
summary: The square, the king in front, the opposition and the rook pawn: the door to pawn endings.
part.square.title: The square of the pawn
part.square.summary: When the pawn runs alone and the black king can't catch it.
part.opposition.title: King in front and the opposition
part.opposition.summary: The double step, the king in front of the pawn, and the kings face to face.
part.draws.title: The draws and summary
part.draws.summary: The rook pawn, stalemate, and the rules to take with you.
step.t_square: Our king is far away and the black king is chasing the pawn. Does it arrive in time, or does the pawn queen on its own?
step.t_square.hint1: Draw a square with one side running from the pawn to its queening square. Can the black king step into it?
step.intro: Almost every pawn ending comes down to this: one extra pawn and the two kings. Knowing at a glance whether it wins or draws is worth a lot of points. Today we ask four questions. Can the black king catch the pawn? Can my king get in front of it? Is it a rook pawn? And, playing Black, where is the stalemate that saves the game?
step.square: First question: can the king catch the pawn on its own? Don't calculate; draw. Run the diagonal from the pawn to the last rank and close the square: here, from g4 to c8. If the black king steps into the square, it catches the pawn. The king on b6 is outside, and it is my move: the pawn runs.
step.squareMove: White to play and win. Run with the pawn and watch the square shrink each move, always one step ahead of the black king.
step.squareMove.hint: Only the pawn. A king move gives the black king the time to step into the square.
step.squareMove.done: A new queen. The black king chased a square that shrank faster than it could walk.
step.t_opposition: The kings face each other, with ours in front of the pawn. Where can the black king go, and what does our king do in each case?
step.t_opposition.hint1: When one king must step aside, the other one advances. See which square our king gains.
step.doubleStep: Watch out for the pawn on the second rank. It may move two squares on its first move, so you count the square as if it already stood on the third: here, from b3 to g8. The king on h5 is outside that square; with the double step, the pawn gets away. With a single step, the king gets there.
step.front: When the king can catch the pawn, my king has to help, and it goes in front of the pawn, not behind it. Here the kings face each other with one square between them: that is the opposition. If Black is to move, the black king has to step aside, and my king walks through on the side it leaves open. If it were my move, I would be the one giving way, and the ending would be a draw.
step.opposition: White to play and win. The black king guards the squares in front of yours. Take the opposition and, when it gives way, walk past it.
step.opposition.hint: Put your king face to face with the black king, one square between them. The pawn waits.
step.opposition.done: That's it. Your king got in front of the pawn with the opposition, and the black king can no longer hold. The key squares lesson takes this road all the way.
step.rookPawn: Now the exception. With a rook pawn, the defending king only needs to reach the corner. From here it never leaves: my king cannot push it off a8 and b8 without stalemating it. King in front, opposition, sixth rank: none of that is enough here. A rook pawn with the king in the corner is a draw.
step.rookPawnMove: Black to play and draw. The pawn is a rook pawn: take your king to the corner, in front of it.
step.rookPawnMove.hint: The goal is c8 or b8. Go along the diagonal before the white king shuts the road.
step.rookPawnMove.done: Done. The black king reached the corner, and nobody can drive it out. A draw.
step.stalemate: The defender's last weapon is stalemate. The black king stays in front of the pawn. When the white king reaches the sixth rank, the black king stands face to face with it. And if the pawn gives check on the seventh, the king steps onto the square in front: to protect the pawn, the white king stalemates it.
step.stalemateMove: Black to play and draw. Stay in front of the pawn and answer every move of the white king.
step.stalemateMove.hint: On the eighth rank, on the pawn's file or next to it. When the white king comes to the sixth, stand face to face with it.
step.stalemateMove.done: Perfect. Now, to save the pawn, the white king must go to c6, and your king has nowhere to go: stalemate.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: the king catches the pawn if it gets into the square; count from the pawn to the eighth rank, and a pawn on the second rank counts from the third. Second: the king goes in front of the pawn, and the opposition decides who gets through. Third: with a rook pawn, the king in the corner draws; as the defender, stalemate is your friend. Here, for example, g3 or g4 only draws: the black king is inside the square. King first.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. The black king is close to the pawn; mine is far away. Bring the king before you push the pawn.
ex.e01: White to play and win. The white king is far away. Can the pawn run?
ex.e01.hint: Draw the pawn's square after your move and see where the black king stands.
ex.e01.solution: b5! The square shrinks to b5–e8, and the black king on g5 can no longer get in. Any king move gives Black the time to step onto f4, f5 or f6 and catch the pawn.
ex.e02: The same position, but now Black is to move. Save the draw.
ex.e02.hint: The square of the b4 pawn runs from b4 to f8. Step into it.
ex.e02.solution: Kf5, Kf4 or Kf6: the three squares on the f-file that are inside the square. The king catches the pawn in time, and the white king, on h1, is too far to help.
ex.e03: White to play and win. Where should the king go?
ex.e03.hint: The king goes in front of the pawn, and it doesn't wait: march forward.
ex.e03.solution: Kd5, Ke5 or Kf5. The king climbs in front of the pawn, to a square the black king cannot reach, and the pawn follows, protected. Retreating or stepping sideways lets the black king take the front and draw.
ex.e04: White to play and win. The pawn can run, but how?
ex.e04.hint: A pawn on the second rank has a special move. Count the square from the third rank.
ex.e04.solution: b4! With the double step, the square runs from b4 to f8, and the king on h5 can't get in. After b3? the square is b3–g8, and the black king steps onto g4, g5 or g6 in time.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The black king guards the squares in front of the pawn.
ex.e05.hint: Opposition first: kings face to face, one square between them. Then walk past on the side the black king opens.
ex.e05.solution: Kf4!, the opposition. The black king has to give way: after ...Ke6, Kg5 gets in front of the pawn on the free side (Ke4 and Kg4 also keep the win). f4? wastes the pawn's move, and the black king stays in front of it: a draw.
ex.e06: An example by Alexander Fishbein. Black has played ...Ke4 and stepped into the square. White to play and win.
ex.e06.hint: The black king wants to reach the pawn along the diagonal. Your king can stand in its way.
ex.e06.solution: Kb4! and, after ...Kd5, Kb5!. The white king climbs next to the pawn and acts as a shield: the black king never reaches it. a5? or any king retreat lets the black king reach the pawn in time.
ex.e07: Black to play and draw. Only one move holds.
ex.e07.hint: The white king wants to climb in front of the pawn. Stand face to face with it.
ex.e07.solution: Kd5!, the opposition. The white king can't climb through c4, d4 or e4, and the draw is safe. Any other move lets the white king take the opposition and walk through.
ex.e08: Black to play and draw. It is a rook pawn. Which road does your king take?
ex.e08.hint: The corner is your salvation, but the white king is racing too. Choose the road it cannot cut.
ex.e08.solution: Kd7! and, after a5, Kc7 (or Kc8, Kd8). The black king reaches c7 and the corner. Kd6? loses: Kb6! and the white king shuts the way to c7 and c8.
ex.e09: Black to play and draw. Use stalemate.
ex.e09.hint: Stay in front of the pawn and meet the white king face to face. When the check comes, step onto the square in front.
ex.e09.solution: Kf8 (or Kf7). After Ke6, Ke8!, face to face with the white king; after f7+, Kf8!. To protect the pawn, the white king must go to f6: stalemate.
ex.e10: White to play and win. A rook pawn: everything depends on which king gets there first.
ex.e10.hint: If the black king reaches f8, it's a draw. Your king can take the square in its path first.
ex.e10.solution: Kg6! and Kg7: the white king gets in front of the pawn and locks the black king out of the corner. After that the pawn walks up on its own. h5? lets the black king reach f8 and the corner: a draw.
ex.e11: Black to play and draw. The natural move loses.
ex.e11.hint: Don't think about the square in front of the pawn; think about the white king. Stand face to face with it.
ex.e11.solution: Ke6!, the opposition: the white king can't climb through d5, e5 or f5. Kd6? looks natural, but Kd4! takes the opposition and the white king gets through.
ex.e12: Black to play and draw. It is a rook pawn, and the white king stands next to it. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: The goal is c7 or c8. Count who gets there first and avoid the squares where the white king cuts you off.
ex.e12.solution: Ke6! and, after a5, Kd7 (or Kd6): the black king reaches c7 and the corner. Ke5? loses to Kc5!, and every other move arrives too late as well.
key.square: The rule of the square: from the g4 pawn to c8. The black king on b6 is outside, and the pawn runs.
key.opposition: Simple opposition: kings face to face, one square between them. Whoever moves gives way. Lichess Practice, Opposition.
key.fishbein: Alexander Fishbein's example (via Wikipedia): the black king gets into the square, but Kb4! acts as a shield.
key.rookPawn: A rook pawn with the king in the corner: a draw, whoever is to move. The white king has no square that doesn't stalemate.
key.stalemate: The defender's stalemate: king in front of the pawn, the opposition and, on the check from the seventh, the square in front.
history: King and pawn against king is the most studied pawn ending, and the one that turns up most often at the end of a game. The rule of the square is in every manual; Wikipedia explains it with a diagram taken from Müller and Lamprecht. Alexander Fishbein, in his 1993 book King and Pawn Endings, showed that getting into the square is not always enough: the other king can act as a shield. Yuri Averbakh taught that the king leads the pawn the way a father leads his child across the street: in front. And the rook pawn has saved even against Fischer: in Zurich, 1959, Barcza was left with his king against Fischer's king and rook pawn, took his king to the corner and drew.
practice: Now the real ending: king on d2, pawn on g2, and the black king inside the square. King first, then the pawn. Pick your time control and go.
